title: Accounting for a US Subsidiary of a Foreign Parent
summary: A US subsidiary of a foreign parent needs US GAAP books and a package the parent can consolidate. See what to produce each month and what to document.
body_markdown:
## Two Audiences for One Set of Books


A US subsidiary of a foreign parent doesn’t have one reporting obligation. It has two, running in opposite directions out of the same trial balance. This page runs one direction only, a foreign parent sitting above a US entity, with the reporting flowing up and out of the US into a group consolidation prepared somewhere else, usually under IFRS. If you’re a US parent translating a foreign subsidiary up into your own consolidation, that’s the opposite problem, and it’s covered in[foreign subsidiary accounting under ASC 830](https://www.indinero.com/blog/foreign-subsidiary-accounting/) .


Downward, the entity owes a US GAAP basis of accounting to lenders, auditors, and anyone underwriting it, plus a federal and state tax filing set that starts in year one. Upward, it owes the parent a package on the parent’s chart of accounts, in the parent’s reporting standard, on the parent’s calendar. They don’t reconcile by accident.


### Why one ledger can’t serve both audiences


No US federal statute compels a private company to maintain US GAAP books. The obligation is contractual and situational. It arrives through bank covenants, a US audit or review engagement, investor rights agreements, and any future US financing or sale. The parent’s IFRS policy manual doesn’t satisfy a US lender who asked for GAAP financials.


It surfaces on the tax return too. Once total assets on Schedule L reach 10 million dollars at year end, Schedule M-3 replaces Schedule M-1 and asks the filer to state the basis the income statement was prepared on. An entity that never produced a US GAAP income statement is reconciling from a number it can’t support.


So the working answer is one basis of record plus a documented conversion layer. Not one ledger trying to serve both audiences at once.


### Functional currency for a US subsidiary of a foreign parent


Functional currency under US GAAP is a matter of fact, not an election. ASC 830-10-45-2 ties it to the primary economic environment in which the entity operates, normally the currency in which it generates and expends cash. For a US operation selling to US customers and paying US employees in dollars, every indicator in ASC 830-10-55-5 points the same way. The dollar is almost always the functional currency, even when the parent reports in euros or yen.


Translation then happens at the parent’s level, not the subsidiary’s. The US entity reports in dollars and books nothing for it. The parent translates under IAS 21, and the reserve lands in the parent’s equity. A parent asking for the package in its own currency wants a presentation convenience, not a functional currency change, so keep that in the reporting layer. For the translation mechanics, see[foreign subsidiary accounting](https://www.indinero.com/blog/foreign-subsidiary-accounting/) .


## Building the Reporting Package the Parent Consolidates


A US GAAP reporting package for a foreign parent is a narrower artifact than a set of financial statements. A group controller is asking for a short list of inputs that feed a consolidation worksheet, on a date certain, in a format that doesn’t need rework. You’re not just producing financials. You’re producing an input to someone else’s close.


### What a group controller actually asks for


1. **A trial balance mapped to the group chart of accounts.** Not the US chart, the mapped one. Keep a US chart that supports US GAAP and the tax return, and own the crosswalk as a maintained artifact.
2. **An intercompany schedule agreed to the counterparty.** Every balance and every intercompany P&L line, with the counterparty named and the number agreed in writing before submission. It’s the line that most often blocks a group close, and the upstream mechanics are in[intercompany eliminations](https://www.indinero.com/blog/intercompany-eliminations-explained/) .
3. **A flux commentary.** Month over month and against budget, written by someone who knows what actually happened in the US business. A variance table with no narrative is a second request.
4. **Supporting schedules for the group’s disclosures.** A fixed asset roll, a lease schedule, a deferred revenue roll, accruals and prepaids, an AR aging, and the intercompany funding roll.
5. **A conversion bridge to the group standard.** Topside adjustments, listed, quantified, and explained.


### Building the calendar backwards from the deadline


Group calendars for an inbound entity commonly land in the working day 3 to working day 5 window. Treat that as what groups ask for, not as a published norm. APQC puts the median monthly close for a finance shared services center at[8.0 days](https://www.apqc.org/what-we-do/benchmarking/open-standards-benchmarking/measures/cycle-time-days-finance-shared) , and APQC data reported by CFO.com puts the median monthly consolidated close at 6.4 calendar days, with top performers at 4.8 days or less.


A parent requesting a mapped, commented, intercompany-agreed package by working day 5 is asking the US entity to close at top-performer speed while also running a conversion the benchmark population never has to run. That isn’t a staffing problem the parent can fix by asking harder. It’s a calendar design problem.


So design the calendar backwards from the submission date:


- **WD4 and WD5.** US GAAP close locked and reviewed, conversion adjustments posted to the reporting layer rather than the ledger, then the package submitted with commentary and bridge attached.
- **WD2 and WD3.** Accruals, prepaids, deferred revenue, payroll, and lease entries posted. Revenue cut-off locked. Intercompany balances agreed with the counterparty in writing.


The rate table and the cut-off convention both have to be settled in writing before the first close. Indinero builds the inbound close calendar backwards from the parent’s deadline, with the rate table, the cut-off, and the intercompany agreement as named steps with owners.


## Where IFRS and US GAAP Diverge on the Way Up


Convergence narrowed the gap between IFRS and US GAAP. It didn’t close it, and an IFRS to US GAAP conversion for a subsidiary bites hardest in the areas a growth-stage US entity transacts in every month.


- **Leases, ASC 842 against IFRS 16.** ASC 842 keeps a dual lessee model, finance or operating, classified against the criteria in ASC 842-10-25. IFRS 16 applies a single model to everything. Under ASC 842-20-25-6 an operating lease produces one straight-line lease cost, where the same office lease under IFRS 16 produces front-loaded expense split between depreciation and finance cost, which moves EBITDA. IFRS 16 paragraph 5 also exempts[low-value assets](https://www.ifrs.org/content/dam/ifrs/publications/html-standards/english/2025/issued/ifrs16.html) and ASC 842 has no equivalent, so laptops the parent expenses, you capitalize. More on the US side in our[ASC 842 guide for private companies](https://www.indinero.com/blog/asc-842-lease-accounting-private-companies/) .
- **Development cost, IAS 38 against ASC 350-40.** IAS 38 capitalizes development expenditure once six criteria are met, whether the intangible is for internal use or for sale. US GAAP expenses research and development under ASC 730 as incurred, with capitalization granted only by specific subtopics, principally ASC 350-40 for internal-use software.[ASU 2025-06](https://storage.fasb.org/ASU%202025-06.pdf) removed the development-stage references from ASC 350-40 and turned capitalization on authorized funding plus a probable-to-complete test that ASC 350-40-25-12A says isn’t met where significant development uncertainty exists. Deloitte’s Heads Up puts the effective date at annual reporting periods beginning after December 15, 2027.
- **Revenue, ASC 606 against IFRS 15.** The five-step models match, which is exactly why assuming convergence is a dangerous shortcut. Collectibility doesn’t match. Probable under IFRS 15 means more likely than not, where ASC 606 reads it as likely to occur at a materially higher threshold and also looks to collection of substantially all of the consideration. A shaky customer can be a contract under IFRS 15 and not one under ASC 606. Our[ASC 606 primer](https://www.indinero.com/blog/asc-606-what-you-need-to-know/) covers the US side.


### The private-company alternatives trap


A US subsidiary of a foreign IFRS reporter usually isn’t a public business entity, even where the parent is listed. So the entity is eligible on its face for the private-company alternatives. A risk-free lease discount rate by asset class under ASC 842-20-30-3. Goodwill amortized straight-line over ten years. The written-terms expedient for common control leases in ASC 842-10-15-3A.


Eligible isn’t the same as advisable. None of those alternatives has an IFRS equivalent. Goodwill amortization is prohibited under IAS 36’s impairment-only model, and a risk-free lease rate produces a liability IFRS 16’s incremental borrowing rate requirement won’t accept. Electing them doesn’t reduce work. It moves the work into the conversion bridge permanently. Settle that question with the group reporting standard in the room, before the first close.


## Intercompany Discipline With the Parent


Every dollar that moves between a foreign parent and its US subsidiary creates three obligations at once. An accounting characterization, a transfer pricing position, and an information return. Treat intercompany flows as internal housekeeping and you generate all three exposures while documenting none of them.


### Agreements and funding characterization


The agreement set is the control. A services agreement defining the services, the cost base, and the markup. A loan agreement with stated principal, rate, maturity, and repayment terms for debt. A board-authorized subscription with shares actually issued for equity. An IP or license agreement where the US entity uses parent-owned IP. All signed before the transactions they govern, because ASC 842-10-55-12 classifies related party leases on their legally enforceable terms.


Debt also has to behave like debt. Stated interest at or above the applicable federal rate, because section 7872 recharacterizes a below-market loan into a loan at the AFR plus an imputed transfer. Accrue the interest and post it. ASC 830-20-35-3 then keeps exchange differences on intra-entity balances of a long-term investment nature out of net income, but only where settlement genuinely isn’t planned in the foreseeable future. Otherwise they hit net income and survive consolidation.


### The cost-plus arrangement and the 30 day clock


Most inbound US subsidiaries are funded by a cost-plus services arrangement. The US entity performs a defined function, invoices the parent for fully loaded cost plus a markup, and books service revenue under ASC 606. That revenue is revenue, not a capital contribution and not a cost reimbursement netted against expense.


The markup is a transfer pricing conclusion, not a plug. IRC section 482 supplies the arm’s length standard, and the documentation that protects against accuracy-related penalties sits in Treas. Reg. section 1.6662-6(d)(2)(iii)(B), which specifies ten principal documents. It has to exist when that year’s return is filed, and be produced[within 30 days of an IRS request](https://www.irs.gov/businesses/international-businesses/transfer-pricing-documentation-best-practices-frequently-asked-questions-faqs) . The accounting team’s job isn’t writing the study. It’s making the books agree with it.


### Form 5472 attaches from year one


Under the[IRS instructions for Form 5472](https://www.irs.gov/instructions/i5472) , a reporting corporation files if it had a reportable transaction with a related party. A 25 percent foreign shareholder is one owning at least 25 percent of the stock by vote or by value. There’s no revenue or dollar threshold, so it can bind in year one for a pre-revenue entity whose only activity was receiving parent funding. File a separate form per related party, attached to the return by its due date including extensions.


The disregarded entity path is the one inbound groups miss. A foreign-owned US DE files a pro forma Form 1120 with Form 5472 attached, on paper, because foreign-owned US DEs can’t file electronically. Determine the obligation at formation. The late-filing consequence is covered at[Form 5472 penalty](https://www.indinero.com/blog/form-5472-penalty/) .


### The practical build nobody budgets for


Standing up the entity has lead times the parent underestimates. Entity formation and a registered agent. An EIN, which gates the bank account and payroll registration. Foreign qualification and payroll tax registration in every state where someone actually sits, covered in[multi-state payroll compliance](https://www.indinero.com/blog/multi-state-payroll-compliance-for-growing-saas/) . A US bank account, where beneficial ownership verification on the parent’s shareholders runs long. And sales tax nexus, which can attach from remote sales volume alone, covered in[startup tax nexus](https://www.indinero.com/blog/startup-tax-nexus/) . Reporting on activity abroad sits in[filing US taxes with foreign activity](https://www.indinero.com/blog/filing-us-taxes-foreign-activity/) .


## Common Pitfalls


The failure modes in foreign owned US subsidiary accounting are predictable, which means they’re preventable. All six below are documentation and calendar failures rather than technical accounting failures, and every one costs more to unwind than it would have cost to set up correctly.


1. **Parent funding posted to suspense with no agreement.** Cash arrives, nobody has a document, and it lands in suspense or in paid-in capital because that balances the sheet. Debt needs a stated rate at or above the AFR and creates interest, withholding, and treaty questions. Equity needs board authorization and issued shares. Decide before the wire.
2. **Running the US books out of the parent’s ERP with no US GAAP review.** This is the most expensive inbound failure, because it produces an entity with no US GAAP position. Not a wrong one. An absent one. The fix is a US GAAP close plus a maintained conversion bridge, built before the first package rather than during the first diligence.
3. **Missing Form 5472.** The obligation attaches in year one because funding moved between the parent and the entity. For a foreign-owned single-member LLC there’s no income tax return already on the calendar to trigger it. Track it as a standing annual deliverable with a per-related-party count.
4. **Intercompany balances that never agree.** The two sides use different rates, different cut-offs, or both. The gap is small in month one, and by month nine it’s a plug account the group audit finds. Agree the schedule with the counterparty before submission, every month, as a close step with a named owner. Our[multi-entity accounting guide](https://www.indinero.com/blog/multi-entity-accounting-guide/) covers the consolidation side.
5. **Assuming the parent’s auditor covers the US entity.** A group audit opinion covers the group financial statements. It doesn’t produce a standalone US GAAP opinion on the subsidiary. What it does produce is work for the US team, component materiality allocated down and a group instruction pack with its own deadlines.
6. **No one in a US time zone able to answer a close question.** A revenue cut-off call comes up during the US business day and the people who can answer it are asleep. The answer arrives tomorrow. In a working day 3 close, that’s a working day gone.


## How Indinero Supports US Subsidiaries of Foreign Parents


What accounting services for US subsidiaries of foreign companies have to cover is three deliverables that agree with each other. US GAAP books. The monthly package the parent consolidates. And the US tax filing set, including the Form 5472 obligation that attaches from year one. Split those across three providers and they drift apart, with the reconciliation landing on the one person at the parent who understands the US entity.


- **CPA-led and GAAP-first.** A US GAAP close performed and reviewed by people whose default basis of accounting is US GAAP, not a group policy manual written for IFRS.
- **One bundled monthly engagement.** Bookkeeping, GAAP close,[business tax](https://www.indinero.com/services/business-tax-services/) , and fractional CFO advisory in one scope, so the structure, the consolidation treatment, and the tax position stay consistent by construction rather than by reconciliation.
- **A close calendar built backwards from the parent’s deadline.** The rate table, the cut-off convention, and the intercompany agreement step are named close tasks with owners, not things that happen if there’s time.
- **A maintained conversion bridge.** The US GAAP position and the group submission both stay producible on demand, and the difference between them is a documented list instead of an archaeology project.
- **A named owner for the US close.** The parent’s team can keep the group submission and the consolidation. Someone still has to own the US GAAP close, the US tax calendar, and the judgment calls that arrive while the US business is open.

## Frequently asked questions


These come up in almost every inbound engagement, usually inside the first two months. They cover the basis of accounting, the currency question, the close deadline, the audit question, and what has to be documented about money moving between the parent and the US entity.


### Do the US entity’s books have to follow US GAAP if the parent reports under IFRS?


Yes, a US subsidiary needs US GAAP books for its lender, audit, and tax purposes, plus a conversion layer feeding the parent’s IFRS reporting. No federal statute compels GAAP books, but bank covenants, a US audit or review, investor rights agreements, and Schedule M-3 all ask what basis the statements were prepared on. Trying to run one ledger that satisfies both standards without a documented conversion layer causes most inbound cleanup work.


### Does a US subsidiary have to keep its books in US dollars?


A US subsidiary selling to US customers and paying US employees almost always has the dollar as its functional currency under ASC 830. Functional currency is a matter of fact, not an election, so it holds even when the parent reports in euros or yen. Translation happens at the parent’s level, not the subsidiary’s. A parent asking for the package in its own currency wants a presentation convenience, so keep that conversion in the reporting layer.


### How soon after month end does a foreign parent usually need the reporting package?


Foreign parents commonly ask for the US reporting package by working day 3 to working day 5, though no standard-setter publishes that deadline. APQC puts the median monthly close for a finance shared services center at 8.0 days, and APQC data reported by CFO.com puts the median consolidated close at 6.4 calendar days, with top performers at 4.8 days or less. Indinero builds the inbound close calendar backwards from the parent’s submission date, with the rate table, the cut-off convention, and the intercompany agreement as named steps.


### Does a US subsidiary of a foreign parent need its own audit?


A US subsidiary of a foreign parent usually doesn’t need a standalone audit purely because of foreign ownership. The real drivers are the parent’s group audit scope, lender or investor requirements, and local statutory triggers. Don’t assume the parent’s auditor covers the US entity, because a group opinion covers the group financial statements, not a standalone US GAAP opinion on the subsidiary. It also pushes component materiality work and a group instruction pack down to the US team.


### Should funding from the parent be recorded as a loan or as a capital contribution?


Parent funding can be either, but the characterization follows the documented intent and terms, so decide and document it before the wire lands. Debt needs a written loan agreement with stated principal, maturity, repayment terms, and interest at or above the applicable federal rate, and the interest has to be accrued and posted. Equity needs board authorization and shares actually issued. Posting the cash to suspense or paid-in capital with no agreement because it balances the sheet is the failure mode worth avoiding.


### What has to be documented about transactions with the parent company?


Three things: signed intercompany agreements, transfer pricing documentation supporting the markup, and the Form 5472 information return filed with the US tax return. Agreements should be signed before the transactions they govern, covering services and the cost base, any loan, and any use of parent-owned IP. Form 5472 attaches from year one with no revenue or dollar threshold, on the 25 percent foreign ownership test measured by vote or by value, with one form per related party.


### Can the parent’s finance team run the US books from overseas?


A foreign parent’s finance team can own the US ledger, but US GAAP review, the US filing calendar, and close-day availability stay open. Running the US books out of the parent’s ERP with no US GAAP review produces an entity with no US GAAP position at all. A cut-off question raised during the US business day also waits overnight when everyone who can answer it is asleep. Indinero’s CPA-led team owns the US GAAP close and the US filing set, so the parent’s team keeps the group consolidation.
